utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is Case Number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, and Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for the appearances, even though the accused are not here. I understand they will be here shortly. For the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Prosecution, it will be myself, Milbert Shin, together with Mr. Michael Johnson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the accused, for Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honour. Attorney Toma Fila and Mr. Petrovic and Mr. Jovanovic appearing for Mr. Sainovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. For Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Tomislav Nisnjic with Peter Robinson and Vojislav Selezan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: John Livingston for Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The accused may sit. We have a number of matters to consider in this Status Conference. Some of them arising from the presence of a new accused. That may require us to revisit some of the dates that we have fixed. I have a list of matters that I will go through, and as I raise them, I'll call on counsel to comment. So counsel will react to the specific questions that I've raised and not speak generally about the matters. I'll start with the pending motions, the preliminary motions. We have a motion from Mr. Sainovic on the form of the indictment. We have a motion from Mr. Ojdanic challenging the jurisdiction in respect of Kosovo and joint criminal enterprise. I have to say that a decision will be given on the latter very soon, most likely next week. The disclosure of supporting material to Mr. Milutinovic was expected to be completed in early February. I understand, Mr. Shin, that that was done yesterday. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct. We completed the Rule 66(A)(i) disclose yesterday. The vast majority of the material had been disclosed on the -- at the initial appearance of the accused or possibly shortly thereafter. There was one item -- one single item that we were not in a position to disclose until either late yesterday or this morning due to some technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Can I just indicate that I received that one remaining item this morning -- or actually when I arrived at the Tribunal building. So I think it's right to say that that disclosure has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I understand that an inquiry has been made as to whether the Trial Chamber would wait until it has received any preliminary motions that Mr. Milutinovic may file, and then determine all the motions together, or whether we will be ruling on the current motions. I am to say that we will rule on the current motions as expeditiously as possible. Motions for provisional release, we have a motion from Mr. Milutinovic for provisional release in respect of which the Prosecution has filed its response. And we have also had a reply from the Defence. What we're waiting on is a medical report which the Chamber requested, and that is due on February 21st. And both the accused Mr. Ojdanic and Mr. Sainovic have now filed further requests for provisional release. And Mr. Sainovic has specifically requested an oral hearing. The responses of the Prosecution to these filings are due on the 24th of February. And I am going to fix Tuesday, March the 11th at 3 p.m. for a hearing of all these provisional motions. Protective measures, we have a motion filed first ex parte then inter partes by the Prosecution for protective measures in respect of nine witnesses, I believe. And the Defence responses to that motion are due on the 18th of February. We also have the review of the Registrar's assessment for contributions in respect of Mr. Sainovic. We had filed last week comments by the Defence, and I'm in a position to say that the decision on that will be given on Monday or Tuesday of next week. There's also the question of an application for a binding order addressed to NATO, to the NATO states, that's from Mr. Ojdanic. And responses from the relevant states are expected at the end of February. I turn now to the question of the pre-trial briefs. I had fixed the 31st of March for the submission of the Prosecution pre-trial brief relating to Mr. Ojdanic and Mr. Sainovic. In view of the fact that any preliminary motion to be filed by Mr. Milutinovic might not be determined prior to that time, that's the 31st of March, it would appear to be good sense to extend the date for the filing of the Prosecution pre-trial brief. And the date that I have fixed is - and I have here calculated reasonable time periods - would be May the 30th or one month after the determination of all the preliminary motions, whichever is the later date. The disclosure of witness statements, the 66(A)(i) statements, disclosure has been completed for Ojdanic and Sainovic apart from some problems relating to the disclosure of material that had been submitted to the confirming judge, Judge Hunt. The Registry has been looking into this matter and has been a facilitator, and I've just been informed that the practical arrangements for that disclosure are in place and proceeding well. So unless I hear otherwise from any of the parties, I take it that that matter has been attended to. As to 66(A)(ii) statements, the Prosecutor has filed a notice of compliance, informing the Chamber that it has made full disclosure with the exception of three sets of statements, the nine witnesses to whom the application for protective measures related, and the nine witness statements not yet available in B/C/S, and the three transcripts of prior witnesses which are said to be not yet available. Mr. Shin, the nine witnesses in respect of whom the application for protective measures has been made, that's understood that you wouldn't be in a position to make disclosure. But for the other two categories, that is, the nine witness statements not yet available in B/C/S and the three transcripts of prior witnesses not yet available, I have in mind fixing March the 31st for disclosure of those two categories of statements. There's just one other matter relating to disclosure, witness statements, Mr. Shin, and it's to fix a date for the disclosure of the witness statements in general. And again, I would fix March the 31st for that disclosure. Expert witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just ask clarification about the point of disclosure of witness statements in general, are you referring to the 66(A)(ii) disclosure for the accused Milutinovic or do you have something else in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be for Ojdanic and Sainovic, and also for Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Expert witnesses, my information is that the Prosecution has indicated that it has not been able to serve two of the expert reports by the date that was fixed, Friday, the 31st of January. And those two are the reports from the constitutional expert and the MUP expert. Mr. Shin, would you comment on that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. We are not yet in a position to disclose those reports, and we will endeavour to do so as soon as that is possible. With regards to the expert reports disclosed generally, just to note that we have of course disclosed these reports and not filed them pursuant to Rule 94 bis, and it may be that that would come at a later stage since the accused may not be in a position at this point to indicate whether they would be wanting to cross-examine those experts or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. With those that have not yet been served should be served by the 31st of March. Would you also comment, Mr. Shin, on the question of the translation of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My understanding, Your Honour, is that there is one translation that is pending a report done by Mr. Phillip Coo, that is pending. And I will have to get back to you on the others if there are any problems with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say it's pending, I mean what do you mean? What's the time frame for it to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I have been told that it will be done by the end of March, if not earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Thank you. Rule 68 disclosure, the Ojdanic Defence had identified six categories of material that the Prosecutor had indicated it would withhold from disclosure under Rule 68 until consent of the Rule 70 provider was obtained. I believe this matter has now been settled by the decision of the Trial Chamber, but it would still leave untouched, Mr. Shin, the disclosure under Rule 68 which is not related to any Rule 70 matter. And that is a question that is outstanding. There is an obligation under 68 to disclose as soon as practicable, but there must be a limit as to the time frame within which the Prosecutor takes to comply with that. Would you comment on that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution is aware of its obligations and is taking all measures to comply with its obligations. If I could just say a few things about the status of the Rule 68 disclosure at this stage, maybe to address first some recent developments. The last Rule 68 report filed in this case was, I believe, on the 10th of October of 2002. That report reflected disclosure made up to and including the 17th of September. Since then, between September and January of this year, a number of additional materials have been disclosed under Rule 68, and some of these -- I could either relate these here or next week we intend to file a new report that would capture all of this material and maybe perhaps that's just as well. We are progressing in our Rule 68 disclosure. Currently we anticipate that there may still be some 1200-person workdays involved in completing the searches, and I'm told by the unit that's in charge of these searches that that constitutes remaining perhaps 25 per cent of the searches that need to be done. A large proportion of those searches are also resulting from some search criteria proposed by the accused Ojdanic which are reasonable, and therefore we have incorporated them into our Rule 68 search criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you translate 1200-person workdays into language that is more understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It's a little difficult to do that due to various work loads. As Your Honour may be aware of the various pools of the staff doing this. There may be some systemic issues that Mr. Johnson will address in relation to the disclosure of Rule 68 materials. I'm not sure that we can give a precise date, but we are still planning to accomplish this in the next couple of months as we had indicated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I will do in view of that is to have this matter reviewed at the next Status Conference, the date for which I'll give shortly. So the next Status Conference, we'll review the question of Rule 68 disclosure. Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wished to draw your attention to the following, and I wish to make a proposal as well. We heard in this courtroom today of a witness statement that would certainly fall under Rule 68. We do not know when the Prosecution came into possession of this material, but in view of the beginning of the trial of Mr. Milosevic, we can only assume that this happened at least a year ago. During this past year, as regards this statement or some of its portions that may fall under Rule 68, we did not get any of this. Therefore, we would be inclined to ask the Trial Chamber to give a deadline to the Office of the Prosecutor, at least with regard to such statements and any other material that the Trial Chamber believes would fall into this category. So relying upon their resources, could they please provide us with such important material so that we could work on our defence properly. What we heard today shows an approach that does not correspond to what the OTP has been telling us all along. We have an important witness statement and a very long period of time during which the OTP has been in possession of this, and we have simply not received this information. As far back as in April last year, on the 26th of April, we made submissions asking for the Defence to receive statements of interalia persons subordinated to General Ojdanic. We have been renewing this request time and again and we have been reassured by the Prosecution that they would grant this request of ours, and we have confirmation from what we heard here today that this request was justified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, I just ask you to respond to what has just been said, that you have been in possession of a particular statement which could fall under Rule 68. And it has not yet been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- as I mentioned earlier, the Prosecution is still in its process of doing its Rule 68 review. There are certain areas that we will intensify our efforts to try to address more rapidly. And with regards to this particular witness statement in question, perhaps I could speak to my learned colleague after the Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, please give some comfort. Yes, Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could just add one point about the Rule 68 procedure, as I understood it Mr. Shin was saying that he hoped that the Prosecution would be able to complete the Rule 68 procedure within about two months, whatever the gobbledygook about 1200-person work hours means. In those circumstances, I don't of course know what date Your Honour is going to set for the next Status Conference, but that could be up to four months away, and I'm wondering whether Your Honour might consider setting a rather more stringent timetable, bearing in mind the Prosecution themselves suggest they should have completed it within two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Livingston. That's an interesting point. Mr. Shin, I had in mind setting the 13th of June as the date of the next Status Conference. Can I confirm that you had indicated that you would expect to complete the Rule 68 disclosure within the next two or three months?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, given the choice between two or three months, it may be wiser for me to offer the three months. Again, we will be taking all measures that we can to comply with our Rule 68 obligations. And if given a deadline, we will promptly inform Your Honour of any difficulties that we may have in meeting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm still inclined having heard all the submissions to maintain the approach that I outlined earlier, which is that I expect the Prosecutor to act in good faith in regard to its Rule 68 disclosure. And I take it that the Prosecutor is doing that. And at the next Status Conference, we will review the matter and if necessary make a ruling on it. The next item is the question of the ongoing disclosure from the Milosevic case. As you might recall, the Trial Chamber had directed the Ojdanic and Sainovic Defence teams to liaise with the Registry to obtain all public transcripts and exhibits in the Kosovo phase of the Milosevic case. I understand that some practical problems have been experienced in this arrangement, and perhaps counsel might want to comment on that. Any comments from counsel on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, today we were told by the Registry that they are working on this and that part of the material which they could not deliver to us by the 31st of January for technical reasons will be delivered within the next few days. However, the issue of the list submitted to us by the Prosecution which represents material that they consider to have disclosed to us, it's a list of 48 pages dated the 31st of January. This list contains numerous elements that depend on the Registry performing their task, and they are to coordinate with the Office of the Prosecutor. However, there is also some material pertaining to the latest report by Phillip Coo which was not been disclosed to us. We see here that these documents exist, but they have not been disclosed to us. And as they are listed here, it is not even clear to me whose obligation it is to disclose them to us. Are we to receive these documents from the Registry or from the Office of the Prosecutor? So perhaps the Prosecutor could inform us of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll have to look into this matter to see whether they are materials that were made a part of Mr. Coo's report, in which case they may be coming with the translation. I'm not sure exactly what material my learned colleague is referring to, but we can certainly assist in trying to identify what the material is and where then perhaps it should best or most efficiently come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, coordinate your efforts with Defence counsel in that regard. I understand that the Ojdanic Defence -- yes, Mr. Visnjic. I understand that the Ojdanic Defence has undertaken the translation of certain documents, including the OHCR reports, and has offered to make these available to other members of the Defence, and I think they are to be commended for that effort. Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just for the avoidance of doubt, as Your Honour pointed out earlier, the previous order about disclosure by the Registry related purely to Sainovic and Ojdanic. Just for the avoidance of doubt, could Your Honour also make the same order in relation to Mr. Milutinovic so that he also can benefit from those -- from that disclosure. Because certainly, I think at the Rule 65 ter conference, that was envisaged, but I haven't seen anything - I stress anything at all - from the Registry. I'm sure there have been technical reasons, but as I say for the avoidance of doubt, I don't think it would do any harm if Your Honour were to make a formal order of joining up Mr. Milutinovic's position with that of the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that, and the Registry will be instructed in coordination with the Defence team for Mr. Milutinovic to ensure that the Defence obtains all public transcripts and exhibits in the Kosovo phase of the Milosevic case. Mr. Shin, I just wanted to raise with you the question of the impact of the surrender of Mr. Milutinovic on the pace of the preparation for trial. Will it affect your preparation significantly, the addition of another accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As Your Honour has already taken into consideration, there will be some impact on the preparation for trial. The -- with the new time line in place, we are otherwise in Your Honour's hands in terms of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What about the number of witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With -- the issue of additional witnesses in relation to the accused Milutinovic is under evaluation right now, and if we choose to add some witnesses, we will make appropriate submissions in that regard. In terms of the overall period of time for the case - though it may be difficult to say at this stage - the only thing we can factor in is additional time for cross-examination which may lengthen the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your original estimate was between 100 to 120 witnesses and three to four months for your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think at the time that we had set out those figures, to put it in the context, as Your Honour will recall, that was a preliminary estimate and based on necessarily the results of negotiations or discussions with the various counsel for the accused relating to the usage of 92 bis as well as prior transcripts and other means of expediting the trial. We don't at this stage anticipate the total number of witnesses to go much beyond that by virtue of the arriving of Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 474 to 479. Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. May I ask any of the parties whether there is any other matter that they wish to raise? Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we wished to draw your attention to some activities which the Defence will undertake in the forthcoming period in order to plan better for the beginning of these proceedings. According to the information we have received so far, the initial disclosure by the Prosecution should be completed by the end of April 2003. It is possible, however, that some of this disclosure will take place at a later date, according to your order, and it's possible that some legal issues will arise which we will submit before the Chamber. Under Rule 70, disclosure was to take place by June 2003, and there is also a motion we have already submitted, and upon disclosure, we will perhaps submit a more specific motion. It's possible that in the end, we will have certain requests for disclosure pertaining to certain witnesses, and we have already made some requests of this nature to the Prosecution. On receipt of the complete material, although we are already working on this as we receive each batch, we will have motions referring to insiders, to fact witnesses, international witnesses, and so on, witnesses from the army, the police, and civilians. And we will request that we be permitted to contact these witnesses in accordance with the established procedure. On receipt of the final report from the Office of the Prosecutor, we shall engage investigators to check their allegations, and we will also make submissions to the Chamber in relation to our visit to Kosovo and to the field. We plan to complete our investigations of Kosovo within six months of receipt of the complete material from the Prosecution, and this we envisage as happening sometime in April 2004. We believe that in this way, we will achieve the following goals: First of all, we shall be able to reach certain agreements with the Prosecution as to certain agreed facts. Secondly, we may be able to carry on the proceedings more efficiently, and finally, we shall be able to make use of some evidence already presented in the Milosevic case including parts of the Defence from the Milosevic case, because so far we have heard only the Prosecution evidence. We will, therefore, refer both to Prosecution and Defence evidence in the Milosevic case. Our position is that this case cannot follow certain precedents such as the Brdjanin/Stakic case in this Tribunal because in this case, Mr. Milosevic was a co-accused with our client and we therefore feel that there is more similarity between these two cases than is the case in some other proceedings where there were parallel proceedings such as, for example, Brdjanin and Stakic or Kordic and Blaskic. Therefore, it is our standpoint that the most efficient way of moving forward would be to complete our investigation after the presentation of Defence evidence and the judgement for the Kosovo part of the Milosevic case. I wanted to submit this to the Chamber so that the Chamber will be aware of our plans and our activities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Visnjic, for alerting the Chamber to your organisational plans. And I encourage all the parties to work together and to adopt all the strategies at their disposal to expedite the proceedings. Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just one more thing that I want to raise myself, which is this: It goes back to Your Honour's order about the provisional release motions, and Your Honour has helpfully set a date for the hearing of those. Can I ask whether Your Honour would be minded to make any directions about any evidence to be heard in the course of those -- hearing those motions because certainly as far as my motion is concerned, the Prosecution already indicated that they would wish to cross-examine witnesses about the guarantees. I imagine the position will probably be the same as regards the other accused as well, in which case the Court might want to have regard to which witnesses will be called, how many are going to be called, and make directions concerning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Livingston. The Chamber will consider that matter and will make any order that is necessary in that regard. Yes, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I had no intention of taking part in the proceedings today, but there is just one question that I would like you to instruct the Prosecution upon by the next Status Conference, that is to say, the 13th of June. Once they disclose all the material, could they tell us who they are going to call as witnesses for the trial itself, and also which witnesses they would like to deal with in some other way because we get heaps of material, we prepare ourselves for all of these persons, and we don't know specifically who they are going to call. Let me be very simple, who are the 100 to 120 witnesses that Mr. Shin and his colleagues would like to call? I would like to find out about that by the 13th of June, please. Also, who will be under Rule 92 bis and so on and so forth. You see, this really expedite matters because then we would only carry out our own investigations in relation to these persons that they are actually going to call as witnesses, and I think this would really expedite matters. Thank you -- oh, yes. As for what Mr. Livingston said, we would also be interested in the following, excuse my language but it would be a waste of time for me if the same people who have already spoken about the guarantees of Yugoslavia or now Serbia would speak about them yet again. This only incurs additional expenses. If the Prosecution is asking them to talk about the same thing time and again for the umpteenth time, we're just going to have an earache but we are not going to hear anything new. Let us hear people who have something new to say, for example, something related to one's state of health or whatever. But calling people yet again to say that they're going to give guarantees and that these guarantees will be valid, I really don't see why. But then of course, that is really up to you, so I would simply like to support what was already said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. As a practical matter, I think -- I know that the Defence would be facilitated if the Prosecutor could identify with precision at this stage the number of witnesses and the witnesses that it intends to call, and also those in respect of which 92 bis would be invoked. But I don't know, Mr. Shin, whether you are able to do that at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for a number of reasons, the Prosecution would not be in a position to do that at this stage. And some guidance, though, along the way may be the 65 ter filing. But apart from that, we certainly couldn't say with any unmovable certainty at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Fila understands the difficulties in presenting a case. The same would apply to the Defence. Mr. Livingston.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one further point that occurs to me out of what Mr. Shin said, it's this: It goes back to the provisional release motions again, that if the Trial Chamber were to consider granting provisional release to one or more of these accused and one of the conditions happened to be not to interfere with witnesses, it could be very important that Mr. Shin and his colleagues are able to identify very clearly who the witnesses are that they intend to call to avoid any sort of accidental interference with a witness who the accused didn't know of or didn't realise was going to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that's a very tangential and incidental connection, but Mr. Shin will no doubt take that into consideration. May I now ask the accused. I'll start with Mr. Ojdanic. Whether there is anything that you wish to raise relating to the conditions of your detention or any matter relating to your health. Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OJDANIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions. I have nothing special to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SAINOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing to raise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Milutinovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to tell something, please, if it would be possible to have private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You would like a private session?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED MILUTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: at 4.14 p.m.
